Occurrences.Kwic: 。咄！瞎漢，三十拄杖少不得。靈雲見桃花。靈雲老，不無端，將謂瞞人返自瞞。千紅萬紫已狼藉，何獨桃花是指南。世尊因文殊至諸佛集處，值諸佛各還本處，唯女人近于佛坐而入三昧。文殊乃白佛：「云何此人得近佛，而我不得？」佛告文殊：「汝但覺此女，令從三昧起，汝自問之。」文殊遶女人三匝，鳴指一下，乃托至梵天，盡其神力而不能出。佛曰：「假使百千文殊亦出此女，定不得下。方過四十二恒河沙國土，有罔明菩薩能出此女定。」須臾，罔明從地而出，作禮世

Senses.Explanation: Manjusri's question about a woman sitting near the Buddha in absorption sets up an old case in which his own powers cannot wake her, while a less exalted bodhisattva can. In the old case, Manjusri finds a woman seated close to the Buddha in absorption and asks why she may approach him when Manjusri cannot. The Buddha tells Manjusri to awaken her and ask her directly. Manjusri circles her, snaps his fingers, and even lifts her to Brahma heaven without success; the Buddha summons Wangming from far below, and one finger snap wakes her. Nanming Huiguang quotes the case in a sequence of old encounters and adds a verse that makes Manjusri's unsuccessful finger snap part of its irony. Hanyu Hongxian quotes the same sequence and answers with a short verse about entering and leaving absorption. Hanxiu Ruqian raises and judges the same case, then gives a separate verse of his own. The three current poems or judgments are independent; the exact question remains Manjusri's one quoted old utterance.

Entries.SourceTerm: 云何此女得近佛坐，而我不得

Senses.PreferredTarget: How can this woman sit near the Buddha while I cannot?
AlternateTargets: Why may this woman sit close to the Buddha, and I may not?
SearchAliases: how can this woman sit near the buddha while i cannot?
why may this woman sit close to the buddha, and i may not?
Senses.Note: Jizong Che retells Manjushri asking the Buddha why the woman may sit close while he cannot. The Buddha sends Manjushri to wake her, but Wangming does so instead; Jizong then adds his own verse about the two figures losing their eyebrows. Manjushri owns the quoted question, Jizong the present verdict. The source-named Bulin Jian raises Manjushri’s question to the Buddha, the failed effort to wake the woman and Wangming’s successful gesture. In his own 拈 he asks why one could release her and the other could not. Manjushri is the quoted questioner; Bulin is the present critic, with no secure roster link. In a hall talk, Xiaoyin Daxin raises Manjushri’s question and the ensuing woman-in-samadhi case. After the old action ends, he lifts his staff and says one string has pierced it all. Manjushri asks the exact old question; Xiaoyin makes the current staff verdict. The case anthology preserves Manjushri’s question and then two distinct named verses, by Yunju You and Tianyi Huai, comparing his failed effort with Wangming’s finger snap. Those poems are useful extra appraisals; they do not make Dahui the speaker of the selected question or turn the old case into two events.

Senses.Explanation: The phrase names a sustained, felt condition of doubt used in inquiry, not a passing uncertainty about a proposition. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly asks what this doubt is and describes it erupting, knotting at the brows, and becoming impossible to put down or drive off. Dahui Zonggao says that while it remains unbroken, life and death press in. Gaofeng Yuanmiao recounts it suddenly arising while he held the question where the one returns, leaving him unable to distinguish directions. Librarian Lai tells Xueyan Zuqin that investigating Chan requires raising it and connects small doubt with small awakening. Preface author Wang Xigun calls not knowing a parent's destination or one's own beginning and end the great doubt of life and death shared across time. Zhongfeng Mingben warns that even uninterrupted conjunction of saying and doubt can become a subtle stealing mind. The corpus thus presents a concentrated condition to be raised and broken, while also warning against treating its continuity as achievement.

The phrase says an exchange leaves everyone under heaven in doubt; 殺 heightens the force of 疑. Fazhu Chang answers his teacher Qi’s question about an earlier trainee’s unresolved doubt, then undergoes further testing in the same encounter. Yingshan Yin applies the phrase to Wang Jingchu’s unsettling conduct with Mi Hu and argues that Wang should have pushed the doubt further. Haiyin Zhaoru says it after raising and leaning on his staff while challenging an assembly to see the dharma king’s appearance. Yunwaize uses it to answer an unnamed questioner asking what Yantou privately revealed to Deshan. The formula names a disturbing uncertainty, not literal killing.
Senses.Note: A forceful expression for provoking or sustaining doubt in a Chan exchange.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (T/T47/T47n1985.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Huizhao of Linji, Zhenzhou. In a direct address to practitioners, Linji Yixuan says that searching for a Buddha, a way, or an ancestor as something to acquire misses the matter. He contrasts genuine understanding with people who merely master texts and then look down on others. He mocks visitors who point at their chests and ribs while claiming to understand Chan and the way, yet cannot respond when tested. Linji says that such people wag their lips everywhere and deceive and clamor through the neighborhoods; he warns that a beating and a fall among the asuras await them. The selected phrase is Linji's present rebuke of public boasting that misleads others, not a neutral report of village speech.

Senses.Explanation: The at-ease person of the Way appears chiefly in the compound “one at ease, with learning ended and nothing contrived,” which the records treat as a named condition rather than mere leisure. Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way". Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived". Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study", and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction", "the ground of actual principle", and this full epithet as different names for "great rest". The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find. The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.
